newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-PNG crisis seen causing capital flight.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-PNG crisis seen causing capital flight.

text.p: Papua New Guinea is sitting on a potential flight of capital which could throw the country back into the economic chaos which led to a full-scale currency crisis in 1994, analysts say.
Mines and other resource projects in this minerals-rich but fragile economy continue to produce, factories still operate, coffee and other agricultural goods still flow through ports.

But an economic backlash is still expected after a week of tension between Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan and rebel army officers angered by Chan's hiring of foreign mercenaries to secure Bougainville Island and the Panguna copper mine.
Some capital would have already left the country in response to the crisis, Satish Chand, PNG specialist at the Australian National University's National Centre for Development Studies, told Reuters.

"The uncertainty itself will have an impact. The international banking system is very sensitive to political uncertainties in the country. I'm pretty sure PNG would have lost a fair bit of foreign reserves by now," Chand said.
Fears also existed that the World Bank and IMF would withdraw support for PNG if stability did not return, he said.
All economic players would be looking for a return to political stability rather than a specific outcome such as the resignation of Sir Julius Chan, he said.
In the meantime, investors would hold back on committing to new projects even though production would continue at existing projects.

The irony in PNG's political crisis is that it has come just as the country was getting back on its feet from a massive economic purge three years ago. Some see the Chan crisis as partly a product of the country's return to economic health.

There are no official figures available in Port Moresby about capital outflows from PNG. The country's unit, the Kina, has so far shown no sign of weakness and is almost unchanged against the Australian dollar since the crisis began.

After a capital flight estimated at about US$400 million because of jitters over budget deficit blowouts, declining per capita aid from Australia and over-ambitious minerals-related economic growth, the Chan government took action in late 1994.
It devalued the Kina by 12 percent then floated the national currency, sending it into a 30-40 percent downward spiral.

Since then budget deficits have been reined back, to 67.4 million kina or one percent of GDP in 1996, inflation has been halved to about 11 percent, interest rates have halved to about 10 percent, debt has stabilised and international reserves have returned to health.

Six months after the 1994 devaluation PNG had only enough reserves to cover imports for a few days. Now they are back to more than 400 million kina, or about six months' worth of imports. Debt was up slightly to 3.7 billion kina at September 30 1996, but this was more a reflection of of the currency devaluation than of increased borrowing.

Chan's hiring of mercenaries to break Bougainville's secessionists and to return the Panguna copper-gold mine back to production after its forced 1989 closure was seen by experts as being too ambitious.
But not all analysts believe that PNG, whose 4.2 million population is sitting on some of the richest gold and copper mines and reserves in the world, is at the brink of new economic disruption.
Professor Ross Garnaut, chairman of the major new PNG gold group Lihir Gold Ltd, which plans to begin production before the end of 1997, said Lihir had not been affected so far.
"We hope that things develop in a way which avoids any effect on our projects or similar projects, but we'll have to wait and see," he said.
John Millett, director of Port Moresby's Institute of National Affairs think-tank, played down the economic effects of the political crisis.
"I don't believe that instability, the minor little political irregularity that we've got here, will have much impact on the economy," he said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
